title: How Railways Changed Everyday Life
summary: Trains did not just carry coal. They brought fresh milk to breakfast tables, letters overnight and whole families to the seaside for the day. They also carried soldiers to war, shaped empires, and inspired painters, poets and songwriters.

sections.heading: Breakfast Came by Train
paragraphs: Picture a big city in about 1820. Thousands of people need milk every morning, but milk goes sour within a day or so, and the fastest way to bring it in from the countryside is a horse and cart bumping along a muddy road. So many cities kept their own cows, crammed into dark sheds in back streets, fed on brewery leftovers and milked right there in town. The milk was often thin, dirty or watered down. Fresh fish was a luxury far from the coast, and fruit and vegetables had to be grown close by or arrive half rotten.

Railways changed the menu. A train could bring milk from farms 50 or even 100 miles away in a few hours, and by the middle of the 1800s 'milk trains' were part of daily life in Britain and the United States. Farmers rolled tall metal milk churns (big cans with lids) to the nearest country station early in the morning. A slow train stopped at station after station, picking up churns, and arrived in the city before most people were awake. Milk trains ran so early, and stopped so often, that 'the milk train' became a joke for any train that was very slow or left at an unbelievably early hour. Later, glass-lined tank wagons carried milk in bulk, a bit like a giant thermos flask on wheels.

Fish travelled the same way. Fishing ports on the coast sent their catch packed in ice on fast overnight trains, so that a fish landed one evening could be sold in an inland market the next morning. In Britain this helped turn fish and chips into a cheap, popular meal for working families in towns far from the sea. Strawberries from Kent, flowers from the Scilly Isles and Cornwall, and early potatoes from the south could all be in London shops within a day.

In the United States the distances were much bigger, and so was the challenge. Huge herds of cattle were raised on the western plains, but most of the people who wanted to eat beef lived in eastern cities. At first, live animals were packed into stock cars and shipped east, which was cruel to the animals and wasteful, since much of each animal could not be eaten. The meat-packer Gustavus Swift had a better idea: butcher the cattle in Chicago and send only the meat east. The problem was keeping it cold for a journey of several days.

In 1878 Swift hired an engineer named Andrew Chase to design a well-insulated, ventilated railway car. The 'refrigerator car', or 'reefer', worked like an icebox on wheels. Big bins called ice bunkers at the ends of the car were packed with blocks of ice, often mixed with salt to make it even colder. Cold air is heavier than warm air, so it sank down from the bunkers and flowed through the meat, while warmer air rose back up to the ice. The ice itself was cut from frozen lakes in winter and stored for months in thick-walled ice houses packed with sawdust and hay.

Railroads were not keen. They earned good money hauling live cattle and did not want to lose it, so Swift paid for the first cars himself and found a Canadian line, the Grand Trunk Railway, willing to haul them. The first car was delivered in 1880, and within about a year Swift had nearly 200. Other companies copied the idea. There were roughly 1,300 refrigerator cars in the United States in 1880 and around 68,500 by 1900, and the national fleet peaked at about 183,000 in 1930.

A long journey meant stopping to top up the ice, roughly once a day, at icing stations along the line where workers shovelled fresh blocks into the bunkers from raised platforms. The Pacific Fruit Express, set up in 1907 by the Union Pacific and Southern Pacific railroads, began with more than 6,000 refrigerator cars and ran its own ice plants; its plant at Roseville, California, could make about 1,200 short tons of ice a day. Thanks to reefers, oranges from California and Florida, lettuce, grapes and peaches could be eaten in New York or Boston in the middle of winter. The way whole countries ate had changed, and the change ran on rails.

sections.heading: Letters and Newspapers Overnight
paragraphs: Before railways, a letter from London to Edinburgh went by mail coach, a horse-drawn coach that changed horses every few miles and still took well over a day. On 11 November 1830, just weeks after it opened, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway carried mail for the first time. Britain's Parliament soon saw that railways were the future of the post, and the Railways (Conveyance of Mails) Act of 1838 required railway companies to carry the mail when asked.

The Post Office then had a clever thought. Why should mail sit in sacks doing nothing during a long train journey? Why not sort it while the train was moving? The result was the Travelling Post Office, or TPO: a railway carriage fitted out as a small post office, with rows of pigeon-holes, sorting tables and clerks working through the night as the train rocked along. By the time the train arrived, letters were already sorted for delivery in the towns ahead.

TPOs even collected and dropped off mailbags without stopping. Beside the track stood tall posts with arms that held leather mailbags. As the train thundered past, a net swung out from the side of the carriage and snatched the bag off the post, while another bag was dropped into a net at the trackside to be collected by the local postman. Doing this at full speed in the dark took great skill and good timing. By 1914 Britain had 126 travelling post office carriages, and many other countries copied the idea.

The most famous celebration of these trains is a short film called Night Mail, made in 1936 by the General Post Office's own film unit. It followed the overnight postal train from London to Scotland, and it ended with a poem by W. H. Auden whose rhythm imitated the beat of the wheels on the rails. British TPOs carried on until January 2004, when the last ones ran and sorting moved to big machines on the ground.

Newspapers rode the rails too. Before railways, a London newspaper might reach a northern town days late. With fast early-morning newspaper trains, a paper printed in the middle of the night could be in shops hundreds of miles away by breakfast. This helped create truly national newspapers, read on the same day across a whole country. People in Cornwall and Cumbria could now argue about the same headlines at the same time, which made a country feel more connected, and helped political ideas, sports results and fashions spread far faster than ever before.

sections.heading: A Shilling to Loughborough: The Day Trip Is Born
paragraphs: In June 1841 a young printer and preacher named Thomas Cook was walking from Market Harborough to Leicester, about 15 miles, on his way to a temperance meeting. The temperance movement wanted people to give up alcohol, which was causing a great deal of misery in poor families at the time. As he walked, Cook had an idea: what if the new railway could carry a big crowd of supporters to a meeting in another town?

He persuaded the Midland Counties Railway to hire him a whole train. On 5 July 1841, about 485 members of the Leicester Temperance Society climbed aboard at Leicester's Campbell Street station and travelled to Loughborough and back, roughly 11 miles each way. The fare was one shilling each. Many of them had probably never been on a train before. There was a band, crowds waved them off, and the day was a huge success.

Cook realised that ordinary working people would happily pay for a day out if someone made it simple and cheap. He began organising more excursions, and soon his trips were not only for temperance meetings. In 1851 he arranged travel for about 165,000 people to visit the Great Exhibition in London's Crystal Palace, a gigantic show of inventions from around the world. In 1855 he led his first tour to mainland Europe, and in the 1870s he even organised a journey around the world. The business he started, Thomas Cook and Son, became one of the most famous travel companies in history.

Cook was not the only person running excursion trains, but he showed how much people wanted to travel just for fun. Seaside towns felt the effect most. Places such as Blackpool, Brighton, Scarborough and Skegness had been small fishing villages or quiet resorts for the rich. Once cheap trains arrived, thousands of factory and mill workers could reach the sea in a few hours. In the cotton towns of Lancashire, whole factories closed for a week each summer (called 'Wakes Weeks'), and entire streets of families boarded trains for Blackpool together. Britain's Bank Holidays Act of 1871 created new public holidays, and on those days stations were packed.

To serve the crowds, seaside towns built piers, promenades, boarding houses, theatres and amusement parks. Blackpool Tower, opened in 1894, was inspired by the Eiffel Tower in Paris. Without the railway, almost none of this would have existed. The same pattern happened in other countries: Americans took trains to Coney Island and Atlantic City, and the French to Normandy beaches and the Riviera.

Railways also changed where people lived. Before trains, most people had to live within walking distance of work, so cities were crowded and packed tight. With regular trains, a clerk could live in a leafy suburb and ride into the city each morning with a season ticket. This daily journey is called commuting. Around London, railway companies actively encouraged it. The Metropolitan Railway even invented a name, 'Metro-land', in 1915 for the countryside along its line north-west of London, and in 1919 it set up a separate company to build housing estates there. Pinner grew from about 3,000 people to around 23,000 in the first three decades of the 1900s. Many of the suburbs where people live today began as fields next to a new railway station.

sections.heading: Hotels on Wheels and the Porters Who Ran Them
paragraphs: Early railway carriages were not comfortable. Third-class passengers in the 1830s sometimes rode in open wagons with no roof, and even better carriages were cramped, cold and hard. On long American journeys that lasted days, travellers had to sit up all night and dash off the train at stations to grab food in a few minutes.

George Pullman, a businessman from New York State who had moved to Chicago, set out to change that. His first sleeping coach was built in 1859 in the workshops of the Chicago and Alton Railroad at Bloomington, Illinois, and in 1862 he started the company that became the Pullman Company. Pullman's cars had seats that folded down into beds at night, with upper berths that swung down from the ceiling, curtains for privacy, carpets, polished wood, fine fittings and, from the late 1860s, dining cars where passengers could eat a proper meal while the countryside rolled past. At its height the company reportedly carried around 26 million passengers a year and was sometimes described as 'the largest hotel in the world', because so many people slept in its cars every night.

Railway companies did not usually own these cars. Instead the Pullman Company owned and staffed them and rented them out, so passengers paid extra for a Pullman berth. And the people who made the whole system work were the Pullman porters. From 1868 the company hired mainly Black men, many of them formerly enslaved or the sons of formerly enslaved people, to make up the beds, carry bags, shine shoes, serve drinks and look after passengers through the night. By the 1920s around 12,000 porters worked for the company, making it one of the largest employers of Black Americans.

The job brought travel, respect in their own communities and a steady income, but the conditions were deeply unfair. Pay was low, so porters depended heavily on tips. Many passengers did not bother to learn their names and simply called every porter 'George', after George Pullman himself, as though they were his servants. According to figures from 1934, porters on regular runs worked more than 73 hours a week on average. They had to pay for their own meals, uniforms and lodging, which could eat up a large share of their wages, and they were not allowed to be promoted to conductor, a job kept for white men.

In August 1925, at a meeting in Harlem in New York City, about 500 porters launched a union, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. Their leader was A. Philip Randolph, a writer, speaker and campaigner who was not a porter himself, which made it harder for the company to fire him. The Pullman Company fought back hard, spying on members and firing men who joined. It took twelve years of struggle, but in 1937 the company finally signed an agreement with the union, giving higher pay and a shorter working month. It is often described as the first major labour agreement between a large American company and a union led by Black workers.

Porters had another, quieter influence. Because they travelled the whole country, they carried news, books and Black-owned newspapers such as the Chicago Defender from northern cities into the South, where such papers were hard to find. They told families about jobs and better lives in the North, which helped encourage the Great Migration, when millions of Black Americans moved north in the early and middle 1900s. A. Philip Randolph went on to become one of the great leaders of the civil rights movement and helped organise the 1963 March on Washington, where Martin Luther King Jr. gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech. A story that began with folding beds on a train ended in one of the most important days in American history.

sections.heading: Railways and Empire: India's First Train
paragraphs: In the 1800s Britain ruled a huge empire, and railways became one of its most important tools. The largest example is India. On 16 April 1853 a train of about 14 carriages, carrying roughly 400 invited passengers, steamed out of Bori Bunder in Bombay (today's Mumbai) towards Thane (then spelled Thana), about 34 kilometres (21 miles) away. It was pulled by three steam locomotives, traditionally named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan. The day was declared a public holiday, a 21-gun salute was fired, and crowds lined the route to watch. The journey took about 57 minutes.

The line was built by the Great Indian Peninsula Railway, a private company based in Britain. To persuade British investors to put up the money, the colonial government gave free land and promised a guaranteed profit of 5 per cent a year, paid out of Indian taxes even if the railway lost money. The routes were chosen mainly to serve British interests: to carry raw materials such as cotton from the interior to ports like Bombay, from where they were shipped to factories in Britain, and to move soldiers quickly to keep control of the country. Most of the locomotives, rails and steel were made in Britain, so British industry profited as well. Indian historians and economists have long pointed out that Indians paid for much of the system but had little say in how it was built.

The engineering was spectacular. Just beyond Bombay rose the steep Western Ghats mountains. Climbing them took years of work on zig-zag lines, tunnels and viaducts; the route up the Bhor Ghat to Poona (Pune) was not completed until 1863, and the other big climb, the Thal Ghat, in 1865. Building such lines was dangerous, and many Indian labourers died from accidents and disease, though exact numbers were never properly recorded. By 1870 a line connected Bombay to Calcutta (Kolkata), right across the subcontinent. In Jules Verne's adventure novel Around the World in Eighty Days, published in 1872, the hero Phileas Fogg crosses India by train, a sign of how famous these new lines had become.

Yet something unexpected happened. The railways, built mainly for the empire, became part of everyday Indian life. Millions of Indian passengers crowded into cheap third-class carriages to visit relatives, look for work, or go on pilgrimages to holy places that had once taken weeks to reach on foot. Mohandas Gandhi travelled third class across India to see how ordinary people lived, and railway journeys helped people from different regions meet, trade and share ideas, including the idea of an independent India. Today Indian Railways is one of the biggest railway systems on Earth and one of the largest employers in the world, carrying billions of passengers a year.

India was not alone. Railways were built across Africa, South-East Asia and elsewhere, often by colonial powers that used them to carry minerals, rubber, cotton and crops to the coast for export. These lines frequently ran from mines and plantations to ports rather than between the towns where local people lived, a pattern that still affects some countries' transport today. As with the transcontinental railroads in North America, railways brought both new possibilities and real harm, and historians try to look honestly at both.

sections.heading: Trains Go to War
paragraphs: As you read in Part 11, the American Civil War (1861 to 1865) showed that railways could decide wars. The North had far more track and factories to make engines and rails, and it used trains to move troops and supplies quickly, while the South's network gradually wore out and fell apart. Generals in Europe studied these lessons carefully.

By the time the First World War began in the summer of 1914, the great powers of Europe had detailed railway timetables ready for war. Germany, France, Russia and Austria-Hungary had each planned, down to the minute, how thousands of trains would carry millions of soldiers, horses, guns and supplies to their borders. Military planners worried that if their rivals mobilised (got their armies ready) faster, they would lose, so these railway plans made it harder to slow down once a crisis began. Some historians argue that the rigid timetables helped push Europe into war; others think this idea is exaggerated. Either way, trains were at the heart of the plans.

In Britain, the government took control of the main railway companies when war broke out, running them through a committee of railway managers so that the whole network worked as one. Trains carried soldiers to the ports, coal for warships, and enormous amounts of shells and supplies. In the United States, President Woodrow Wilson put the railroads under government control on 26 December 1917, creating the United States Railroad Administration to untangle traffic jams of freight and make the system work as a single network until 1920.

Near the front lines in France and Belgium, big trains could not go close to the trenches, because their smoke and steam gave away their position to enemy artillery. So both sides built small 'trench railways' with track only 60 centimetres (about 2 feet) apart. These light railways could be laid quickly and carried ammunition, food, building materials and water up to the front, and brought wounded soldiers back. France had developed this gauge, made popular by the Decauville company, and the British, Americans and Germans used the same size. Britain needed so many small engines that it ordered 495 from the American company Baldwin. Horses and mules still did a huge amount of carrying, and hay and oats for them were the single largest type of cargo Britain shipped to France during the war.

Railways also carried the wounded. Ambulance trains, with beds, medical staff and small operating areas on board, took injured soldiers from the battlefields to hospitals and to ships waiting at the Channel ports. Over the course of the war, ambulance trains carried many hundreds of thousands of wounded soldiers away from the fighting. For many soldiers, a train was the last thing they saw before the front and the first sign that they were on their way home.

sections.heading: Big Business, Wires Alongside the Track, and Trains in Art
paragraphs: Railways did not only change daily life. They changed how the modern world was organised. Running a railway was unlike running a farm or a small workshop. A big American railroad in the late 1800s had thousands of miles of track, tens of thousands of workers, hundreds of stations and trains running day and night. Nobody could simply keep an eye on everything personally. So railway managers invented new ways to run huge organisations: departments with clear jobs, written rules, timetables, regular reports sent to head office, careful accounting of costs per mile, and chains of managers. Historians often say that railways created the modern big company, and other businesses, from steel makers to department stores, copied their methods.

The size of it all was astonishing. The United States had about 9,000 miles of railroad in 1850. By 1900 it had roughly 190,000 to 200,000 miles, and the total peaked in 1916 at around 254,000 miles, more than enough to wrap around the Earth ten times. Around 1920 American railroads employed about 2 million people. Railway shares were bought and sold on stock exchanges, and railway companies became some of the first businesses owned by thousands of shareholders.

Railways also pushed industry towards standard parts and shared rules. Engines and wagons from different companies had to be able to run on each other's tracks, so gauges, couplings and brakes gradually became standard. In the American South, many lines used a 5-foot gauge, and in 1886 most of them were converted to standard gauge in a gigantic coordinated effort over just a couple of days, with gangs of workers shifting one rail inward along thousands of miles of track. The telegraph followed the railway too. Telegraph wires were strung on poles beside the tracks, so the railway's right of way became a highway for messages as well as trains, carrying news, business orders and the time signals you met in Part 13.

Artists noticed that the world had changed. In 1844 the British painter J. M. W. Turner showed a painting called Rain, Steam and Speed: The Great Western Railway. It shows a dark locomotive with a glowing firebox racing towards the viewer across Brunel's bridge at Maidenhead, blurred by rain and mist, and Turner sneaked in a small hare running ahead of the train. Some people read the hare as a race between nature and machine. In 1877 the French painter Claude Monet painted a whole series of pictures of the smoky, sunlit Gare Saint-Lazare station in Paris.

Writers and musicians joined in. Edith Nesbit's 1906 children's book The Railway Children is about three children who move from London to a house in the countryside, where their lives revolve around the railway line nearby. Americans sang ballads about Casey Jones, an engine driver who died in a crash in 1900 while trying to stop his train in time, and about the steel-driving man John Henry, a figure of legend who raced a steam drill while digging a railway tunnel. Blues musicians copied the rhythm and whistle of trains on guitar and harmonica. Luxury trains such as the Orient Express, which began running from Paris in 1883, became settings for mystery novels. Railways had become part of how people imagined the world.

By the early 1900s, cities had grown so big, partly because of railways, that their streets were jammed with horses, carts, buses and people. The trains themselves could not squeeze any further into the crowded city centres. So engineers began to look in a new direction: down. Our next stop is underground, in the smoky tunnels beneath London, where a new problem needed a new kind of power.

deepDive: Historians have argued for decades about how much railways really mattered to economic growth. In 1964 the American economist Robert Fogel published a famous study asking a 'counterfactual' question: what would the US economy of 1890 have looked like if railways had never been built, and goods had travelled by canal, river and wagon instead? His answer surprised many people. He estimated that the direct savings from railways for moving farm goods in 1890 were only a few per cent of the nation's total income, and that canals and roads could have done much of the job, more slowly. Fogel later shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in economics, partly for this kind of number-crunching history. Critics replied that his method missed the bigger effects: railways shaped where cities grew, created national markets, pushed the steel and coal industries, invented modern management and moved people as well as goods. Speed itself had value that is hard to count. Most historians now accept that railways were enormously important, while agreeing with Fogel that no single invention is ever truly 'indispensable'. The debate about railways and empire is even sharper. Supporters of the British Raj once pointed to India's railways as a gift of modern technology. Many Indian economists and historians answer that the system was paid for largely by Indian taxpayers, built with guaranteed profits for British investors, designed to move raw materials to ports and troops to trouble spots, and stocked with British-made equipment. Some studies suggest the railways did help reduce the impact of local food shortages by letting grain move between regions, while others note that grain could also flow out of hungry areas towards richer markets. Both effects can be true at once. Finally, social historians stress that the railway changed experiences of time and space. A worker in Leicester in 1841 could, for the first time, see the sea and be back home the same day. Ice-cooled meat from Chicago meant a family in Boston no longer depended only on local butchers. These everyday changes are harder to measure than miles of track, but they may be the railway's most lasting legacy.
funFact: Many Pullman passengers called every sleeping-car porter 'George', after the company's founder George Pullman, whether that was the porter's name or not.
